source: Zhang, Gu, Chen, Ding, Chai, Fan (2025) Leveraging LLMs to Emulate the Design Processes of Different Cognitive Styles
finding: Full text read. GPT-4o was prompted (zero-shot CoT) to act as a problem-driven or solution-driven designer. Its traces were coded with the FBS scheme. Static issue shares matched humans. Cross-space transitions did not: the problem-driven persona made FEWER problem-solution (PS, SP) switches than the solution-driven persona.
numbers: 4 groups x 10 generated processes (P1,P2,S1,S2) plus 2 baseline groups x 10 (B1,B2); bathroom-product task, with and without extra constraints. Without constraint: PS 6.7 vs 10.5 (p=.001), SP 6.4 vs 9.8 (p=.003), SS 9.9 vs 29.4, PP 30.7 vs 15.3 (p<.001). With constraint: PS 8.7 vs 10.4 (p=.333), SP 8.2 vs 9.5 (p=.471). Reformulation-S 5.8 vs 21.5 (p<.001). Both personas beat baseline on novelty and integrity (p<.05); solution-driven had higher integrity than problem-driven. Coders agreed 79.5%; two experts' ratings r=.77.
quote: LLMs still need improvement in emulating complex nonlinear transitions between problem and solution spaces
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one product task, 10 runs per cell, 2 expert raters, no token control (persona text is extra context), no test of whether transition complexity predicts quality. Outcome gain is persona vs bare prompt, not process order vs process order.
agent_relevance: An LLM told to be problem-first does not loop back on its own. Cross-space returns must be forced by the scaffold, not requested in prose. A visible design process also raised novelty over a bare prompt, so it is not harmful for open-ended output.

source: Luan et al. (2026) Repair or Resample? Rethinking Failure Debugging in LLM Multi-Agent Systems (SymTrace, SymFail)
finding: At an equal three-attempt budget, generic feedback (self-reflection, critic) did NOT beat a plain unguided rerun. A single intervention at the node where a concrete failure symptom was detected beat all of them by a wide margin.
numbers: 536 human-annotated failed Web-agent trajectories, three MAS frameworks. Repair rate (pass@3 for task-level, pass@1 for node-level): unguided rerun 6.90%, self-reflection 4.29%, critic agent 3.73%, random-node intervention 3.73%, suspicious-node (symptom-triggered) 20.15% (108/536). Unguided rerun reproduced the source failure only 67.97% of the time.
limits: Web-agent tasks with outcome checks, not design or frame revision. Symptom detector and repair prompt are tested jointly. Repair is of a recorded failure, not a problem restatement. LLM judges used for symptom scoring.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 6: what triggers the return matters more than having one. A localized, evidence-based symptom beats a generic reflect-and-retry, and plain resampling is a strong equal-budget baseline. Our S3-to-S2 test must include a resample-only arm.

source: Cash, Goncalves, Dorst (2023) Method in their madness: Explaining how designers think and act through the cognitive co-evolution model
finding: A quantitative protocol test of co-evolution (Dorst is an author). Transitions between problem and solution were tied to the designer's perceived uncertainty, counted as hedge words per segment. Higher uncertainty marked a change of transition type.
numbers: Reanalysed dataset of 31 novice master students (10/11/10 across three stimulus conditions), 45-min think-aloud sessions on a child-sleep product brief, 1617 segments. Uncertainty level vs transition: chi2(6, N=1617)=180.1, p<.001; change in uncertainty vs transition: chi2(6)=30.0, p<.001. Uncertainty level in segments where the transition type changed: Welch t=-3.905, p<.001; change in uncertainty: t=-1.568, p=.117 (ns). Logit for transition change: LR chi2(2)=16.11, pseudo R2=.0101; level coef .1050 (p<.001), change coef -.0289 (p=.151).
limits: Novices, one brief, correlational. Hedge-word count is a crude uncertainty proxy. Pseudo R2 about 1%, so the signal per segment is weak. The nine-designer professional data of Dorst and Cross 2001 were not re-tested. No quality scores tie the transition pattern to outcome quality.
agent_relevance: A usable trigger for a reframe is a solution-side uncertainty signal (hedging, low confidence). It matches the stall and failed-check triggers in gap 6. The effect is small, so pair it with a check. First quantitative segment-level test of co-evolution seen.

source: Xu et al. (2026) metacognitive co-regulation design agents (Ralph Wiggum Loop, SRL, CRDAL), arXiv 2603.24768, step and cost data
finding: Re-read for cost. The runs were not near the 30-step cap: all three systems stopped after about 9 steps on average, and step counts did not differ. Monitor-agent calls and tokens were not measured, so equal-token is still untested.
numbers: Mean design steps per run (30 runs each): RWL 9.07 (SD 7.02, range 2-30), SRL 9.10 (SD 4.45, 4-27), CRDAL 9.37 (SD 3.20, 3-17). ANOVA F(2,87)=0.031, p=.97, partial eta2=.001. Capacity: SRL vs RWL t(40.6)=3.715, p=.001, d=.956; SRL vs CRDAL t(57.8)=2.888, p=.005, d=.746. Model: Gemini 3.1 Pro preview, one battery-pack task. Authors count cost in steps because simulation cost dominates.
limits: Refines the critique: steps are equal in outcome, not merely capped. But tokens per step differ because the monitor adds calls. One task, one model, no best-of-N arm.
agent_relevance: The gain is better described as same number of design iterations with different guidance, which is the right unit if evaluation (a simulator) is the cost. Under a token budget the claim is still open (gap 8 stays open).

source: Deng et al. (2023) Rephrase and Respond, model-strength results (Sec 4.3, 5)
finding: Self-rephrasing helped the strongest model most. Weaker models gained little and sometimes lost on some tasks. A strong model rephrasing for a weak one helped the weak model more than its own rephrase did.
numbers: Text: GPT-4 gains on all tasks; GPT-3.5 and Vicuna-13b slightly diminished on Sports. Vicuna answering own rephrase vs GPT-4 rephrase: Even day 58.10 vs 61.90, Even month 56.19 vs 60.95, CSQA 51.36 vs 55.00, Sports 65.00 vs 73.64, Dates 32.79 vs 37.67, Last letter (2) 5.45 vs 10.45.
limits: Only 10 short checkable tasks. Vicuna-13b has near-zero skill on some. No token match against extra sampling.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the frame step is not free for a weak model. On a weak model, skip self-framing or let a stronger model frame. Test as a scaffold switch keyed to model tier.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025), expert-novice results
finding: Experts, measured by a reframing quiz, produced more novel frames than novices when working with an LLM. The free-form gap was larger but not significant. Usefulness showed no group differences. The authors read this as LLMs widening the competence gap.
numbers: Novelty of LLM-conditioned frames: experts 12.54% more novel than novices (Z=2.70, p=.01). Free-form gap 20.84% (Z=2.31, p=.06). Usefulness: all p>.05. Frames rated by 15 high-expertise participants. No LLM arm beat the baseline on novelty or usefulness.
limits: Expertise is the person's, not the model's. The comparison is among LLM arms, so it does not show whether experts also beat novices without an LLM. Experts rated the frames, so the null may partly reflect strict rating.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 for the human steering the agent: skilled users get more from frame output. For a schema, that argues for a check step by the user or a verifier, not for dropping framing.

source: Brunzema et al. (2026) Agentic Bayesian Optimization through Surrogate-Augmented Autoresearch (Sara)
finding: An LLM agent can revise strategy and even reformulate the problem mid-run without restarting. The reformulation demo was triggered by an instructor changing the requirement, not by a failed solution attempt. Model capability mattered mainly for tool use.
numbers: Reformulation demo: scaling-law study, compute promoted from constraint to second objective, acquisition switched to hypervolume, all earlier trials reused. Model ablation (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5): Haiku under-performs on Ackley-10D, smaller gaps on LCBench and Mizoroki-Heck. GPT 5.5 vs Opus 4.8: GPT uses about 1.5-2x more tokens on some benchmarks.
limits: Reformulation shown as one trace excerpt, no controlled test of reframe vs fixed problem, no equal-token comparison; the paper says it does not optimize cost.
agent_relevance: Shows S3-to-S2 revision is feasible when an append-only trial log keeps old evidence valid under the new frame. Design rule: keep raw attempts as the source of truth so a reframe does not discard data. Not evidence that the return pays.

source: Allaham et al. (2026) Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
finding: Even on a checkable task (Lean specs, verifier-scored) clarification questions were not a uniform gain. The same-model pipeline lost; some cross-model pipelines gained a little; a larger question budget (10) did not beat 3.
numbers: 189 Verina tasks. Single-shot baselines 59.3% to 63.5% strict pass@1. Sonnet 4.6 same-model: -2.6 pp (-5 tasks) at k=3, -4.2 pp (-8) at k=10. Sonnet 4.6 to GPT-5.6: +6.3 pp (+12) at both budgets, bootstrap lower bound near zero. To Gemini 3.8 Flash: +4.8 pp (+9). To Claude Sonnet 5: +1 task at k=3, -6 tasks at k=10. Failures concentrated in postconditions.
limits: Simulated developer answers come from the reference. Extra calls not token-matched. Pipelines rerun per configuration, so cross-model differences are not isolated.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the clarify step is fragile even where a missing fact exists. For open-ended design, where no single fact is missing, expect weaker transfer. Cap questions low and do not assume more is better.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without an outside check, extra self-correction rounds lowered accuracy, and each round lost more. With an oracle label deciding when to correct, the same loop gained.
numbers: GPT-3.5 (GSM8K / CommonSenseQA / HotpotQA): standard 75.9 / 75.8 / 26.0; self-correct round 1 75.1 / 38.1 / 25.0; round 2 74.7 / 41.8 / 25.0. GPT-4: standard 95.5 / 82.0 / 49.0; round 1 91.5 / 79.5 / 49.0; round 2 89.0 / 80.0 / 43.0. Oracle-triggered: GPT-3.5 84.3 / 89.7 / 29.0, GPT-4 97.5 / 85.5 / 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changed correct to wrong more often than wrong to correct.
limits: Oracle labels are not available to a real agent; the oracle row is an upper bound for failed-check triggers. Reasoning-only tasks, 2023 models. Table text was extracted from a garbled layout; the row mapping is by order.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6: a reframe loop that judges itself drifts and degrades after 1-2 rounds; a reframe gated by an external failed check is the version that can pay.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Refine rounds helped on average with diminishing returns, up to 4 iterations, and not always monotonically on multi-aspect tasks.
numbers: Code optimization 22.0 to 28.8 after 3 iterations; sentiment reversal 33.9 to 36.8; constrained generation 29.0 to 49.7. Max 4 iterations used. Acronym generation quality varied across iterations; the best-scoring iteration is chosen.
limits: Tasks with clear style feedback, not problem reframing. Compute not matched to sampling. The Huang critique applies to reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: measured gains come mostly in the first 1-3 rounds. Use a hard cap of 2-3 reframe rounds by default and keep best-so-far.

source: Kokotovich (2015) A Case for Reimagining Reflection-in-Action and Co-evolution (IASDR 2015), summary of Kokotovich 2008
finding: The author's own later summary of his 2008 study lists five qualitative findings about students using non-hierarchical mind maps in the problem stage: more and better-articulated design issues early go with more creative final proposals. No numbers are given.
numbers: No sample sizes or statistics in this paper.
limits: Secondary, by the same author, an argument paper. The 2008 original (Design Studies 29(1):49-69) is closed access and was not obtained. The findings are within-group correlations, not a test of problem-first against solution-first.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: the map-the-problem-first critique rests on correlation in one student mind-map study. Do not treat it as a causal order effect when setting the S2 depth.

source: Kokotovich (2008) Problem analysis and thinking tools: an empirical study of non-hierarchical mind mapping (Design Studies 29(1))
finding: Abstract page only (full text closed access). Experiments with first-year industrial design students found statistically significant correlations between the analysis phase and creative output.
numbers: No N or statistics in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Correlational. Tool-based problem analysis, no solution-first control arm.
agent_relevance: Cannot support a numeric order effect. Gap 2 numbers remain unavailable.

source: Kruger and Cross (2006) Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes (Design Studies 27(5):527-548)
finding: Abstract as reported by a search result; the repository page was blocked by a bot check. Nine experienced industrial designers did the same task; four strategies were identified (problem-driven, solution-driven, information-driven, knowledge-driven). Solution-driven designers had lower overall quality but higher creativity scores; problem-driven designers had the best balance of quality and creativity.
numbers: N=9 designers (same data as Dorst and Cross 2001). Group means and tests not obtained.
limits: Not opened. With 9 designers split over four strategies, cells hold 1-4 people. Strategy was labelled after the fact, not assigned.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the only human order comparison on outcomes says solution-first buys creativity at a cost in quality, problem-first balances both. The cells are tiny, so use it as a hypothesis for an LLM test, not as a rule.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution (Design Studies 22(5):425-437)
finding: Abstract page only; full text not reachable (host unreachable, search quota used up). Protocol studies of nine experienced industrial designers, designs rated for overall quality and creativity; the authors say the co-evolution model generally holds and add default and surprise spaces. No inferential statistics seen in any source.
numbers: N=9 designers, one task. No replication with numbers found in any source seen this session.
limits: Abstract only. The same nine-designer dataset feeds Kruger and Cross 2006. Cash et al. 2023 (d03) is the nearest quantitative test, on 31 novices and a different brief.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open on exact numbers. The model is supported by newer segment-level data (d03) but not replicated on the original expert data.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Comparing the design cognitive process between problem-driven and solution-driven industrial design students (Int J Technol Des Educ 33:557-584)
finding: Abstract page. 54 students split by the FBS P-S index. Problem-driven students keep stating the problem; solution-driven students develop structure. Style was stable across conditions. Constraints raised solution-driven students' process intensity, with a more complicated effect on problem-driven students. No outcome-quality result in the abstract.
numbers: N=54. No other numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Outcome quality not reported there. Zhang et al. used this paper as the human benchmark.
agent_relevance: Human benchmark for FBS coding. Gap 7 comparison point: problem-driven humans show many PS/SP switches, the LLM persona did not (d01).

source: Huang et al. (2024) debate vs self-consistency (same paper, Sec 4 and Table 7)
finding: At equal numbers of model responses, simple majority voting beat multi-agent debate on GSM8K. Equal-budget baselines matter.
numbers: Standard 1 response 76.7; debate round 1 (3 responses) lower than self-consistency 3 responses 82.5; debate round 2 (6 responses) 83.2 vs self-consistency 6 responses 85.3; self-consistency 9 responses 83.0 to 88.2 in the extracted table (columns garbled).
limits: GSM8K only, one model family. Table columns were garbled in extraction; only the debate-below-voting ordering is relied on.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: compare the S3-to-S2 return with a vote or resample arm at equal tokens, not only with a single pass.

source: Luan et al. (2026) Repair or Resample? regression of successes (same paper)
finding: Rerunning a task can break a run that had passed. A reframe loop that re-enters after a pass risks the same.
numbers: 54 first-pass successes rerun 3 times each: 162 reruns, 85 failed, and 39 of 54 cases failed at least once.
limits: Web-agent tasks, outcome-checked, specific frameworks.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: add a stop rule so the loop exits when a check passes; never reframe a verified answer.

source: Ask Less, Ask Better (2026) Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets, arXiv 2610.24411
finding: Listing snippet only. Limiting an agent to 1-3 clarifying questions cut user-attention cost 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of task reward.
numbers: 36-73% cost cut, 86-94% reward kept (from listing).
limits: Not opened. Task types unknown.
agent_relevance: Supports a small question cap (gap 9) but needs reading before use.

source: Knowing When Not to Answer (2026) Cross-Domain and Multi-Turn Generalization of Latent Underspecification Signals, arXiv 2610.08413
finding: Listing snippet only. Probes flag underspecified questions (math AUROC 0.77-0.97) but a gate on the probe does not reliably beat plain generation. Authors say the gap is in using the clarification, not detecting the need.
numbers: 423-conversation multi-turn benchmark; AUROC 0.77-0.97 on math.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: detecting missing information is easier than benefiting from the answer; spend schema effort on the use step.

source: Cash et al. (2023) Method in their madness, idea-output result (same paper)
finding: Idea outputs were created in segments with distinct uncertainty levels and transition types, so the loop is tied to output, not only to talk.
numbers: Idea creation vs uncertainty level chi2(2, N=1617)=200.6; vs change in uncertainty chi2(2)=65.3; Welch t=-12.174 (level) and -10.082 (change), all p<.001; vs transition type chi2(3)=382.8.
limits: Same novice dataset; whether ideas were good was not the test.
agent_relevance: Output appears where the designer is uncertain, so uncertainty is a candidate signal for switching space.
